newsitem.title: GERMANY: German media gear up to mark Kohl record.
newsitem.headline: German media gear up to mark Kohl record.

text.p: Helmut Kohl still has seven weeks to go before setting the record as Bonn's longest-serving postwar chancellor, but the German media are already extolling him as a man of historic stature.
ARD television got a jump on its competitors on Wednesday evening with a relaxed hour-long chat, the first time in his 14 years in power that Kohl has appeared on a German talk show.

Two more TV appearances, a book, a photo exhibition and countless articles and broadcasts are set to sing his praises until October 31, when Kohl, 66, finally breaks the record set by his political mentor Konrad Adenauer.

"Apart from Queen Elizabeth, no other figure of European history at the end of this century has such a rich experience and rank as Kohl," the Rheinischer Merkur weekly commented in one of the more unusual comparisons being made.

Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung dubbed him "the master of the airwaves" and said Kohl, once one of Germany's least telegenic politicians, had since learned how to dominate the medium like no other leader here.

On October 31, his 5,145th day in office, Kohl will break the record Adenauer set as West Germany's first chancellor between 1949 and 1963. The hefty Christian Democrat became chancellor on October 1, 1982.

The symbolism will be more than just numerical. Kohl has always seen himself as "Adenauer's grandson" and his work reuniting Germany and pushing forward European integration as the continuation of his mentor's policies.
He carefully ducks the inevitable question whether he is now aiming to break the absolute record -- the 19 years that "Iron Chancellor" Otto von Bismarck ruled in Berlin.
Kohl overshadows other German and European politicians in so many ways -- in his massive physique, unmatched experience and political cunning -- that his shortcomings seem to pale.

Several newspapers ran long and favourable articles on Thursday about the chancellor's talk show premiere. That two opinion polls this week showed his government now lagged behind the opposition in popularity rated only a paragraph or two.

The chancellor, who is sometimes testy or unsure when being quizzed for a television news show, comes across as a jolly father figure when chatting with a friendly interviewer like his chat show host Alfred Biolek.
"Kohl dissects history into a casual series of stories," the Sueddeutsche Zeitung wrote in admiration. "He turns statesmen into suppliers of anecdotes."
Biolek, for example, wanted to know from Kohl what he and Boris Yeltsin talked about when they were in the sauna on the chancellor's earlier visits to the ailing Russian president.
"Certainly not about our good looks!" Kohl laughed.
Later, looking more sombre, he spoke of conversations about death and God with the late French President Francois Mitterrand.

This well-timed "Chancellor Festival", as the weekly Die Woche described the publicity wave, is hardly a coincidence for a leader as careful as Kohl. It comes just as he is pushing an unwelcome austerity package through parliament.

"Kohl has learned to ration his television appearances," the Sueddeutsche Zeitung said. "He knows anyone who appears too often gets worn out. Kohl tours through televisionland every two years and almost disappears in-between."
